lesson.menu_desc: Sell something to the person who can say yes -- used to and would
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 5 -- Pitching the Idea
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Pedro Henrique Tadeu Alves da Silva | Lesson 5 -- Pitching the Idea
lesson.grammar_point: used to and would for past habits

listenings.text: I sit on the other side of the table, so let me tell you what happens in my head in the first thirty seconds. I am not listening for your idea. I am listening for whether you understand the thing you want me to change. If you open by telling me how the process works today, and you get it right, including the boring part that everyone forgets, then I relax, and everything after that lands differently. If you open with the solution, I spend the rest of the meeting checking whether you actually know the problem, and I stop hearing you. The second thing I listen for is what it costs me. Not money, necessarily. Time, attention, one person I would have to move off something else. Anybody who names that cost before I do has already won half the argument, because it means I am not going to find it later on my own. And the third thing, honestly, is whether you have thought about what happens when it does not work. Nobody signs off on something that has only one ending.

We used to run the auditions on paper, and I mean actual paper. Four thousand people would send a video, and a team of six would sit in a room for three weeks with printed sheets, and every one of those sheets had a name written by hand. It worked, in the sense that a shortlist came out at the end. But the lead time was three weeks, and the bottleneck was always the same: one person had to watch everything before anyone else could start. So I built a small version of a new system, for one category only, and I did not ask anybody for a budget. That was the whole trick. I built the proof of concept on two weekends, showed it running with real videos, and then asked for the money. The first answer was still no. Somebody pushed back and said the team would never use it, and that was a fair objection, so we ran it beside the paper for one season. That was four years ago. Nobody has printed a sheet since.
